title: Researchers: Look for a smaller dead zone in the Chesapeake Bay this summer
summary: Drought conditions this year may have hurt crops and strained drinking water supplies, but there’s an upside: Low river flows mean less nutrient runoff into the Chesapeake Bay, which could make this year's annual “dead zone” one of the smallest on record.
content:
By Jeremy Cox

The drought that has plagued much of the Chesapeake Bay’s watershed during the first half of this year is causing strains to drinking water supplies, hurting crop output and leaving many rafters and boaters high and dry.

But there’s an upside. Low river flows during the late winter and early spring led to reduced amounts of nutrient pollution flowing into the Chesapeake Bay. As a result, scientists say, the Bay’s annual “dead zone” could rank among the smallest on record.

Dead zones are areas where the oxygen level in the water is so low that it can kill aquatic life, including blue crabs and fish. The zones form naturally in the summer when warming water temperatures mix with the nutrients nitrogen and phosphorus to fuel algae blooms, which rob the water of oxygen when they die.

But decades of land-based problems, such as overfertilized agricultural fields and a lack of urban stormwater treatment, have caused the bay’s dead zones to mushroom in size.

Chesapeake blue crab population drops 50%. The question is: Why?

This year’s dead zone-afflicted area is expected to be among the lowest 10% in size since widespread monitoring began in 1985, according to a forecast by William & Mary’s Batten School, the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, FlowWest and the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science.

From January through April, river flows entering the Bay were down 32% compared to the long-term average. That helped lower nitrogen inputs 39% below the typical amount, the researchers said. Overall, the dead zone is projected to be 31% less extensive than average later this year.

“This mild year for dead zones is good news, especially compared with years when high river flow and nutrient loads have fueled much longer-lasting and larger areas of low-oxygen conditions,” said Peter Tango, monitoring coordinator with the U.S. Geological Survey at the Chesapeake Bay Program.

But other conditions could change the outcome, they cautioned. Weather during the summer – including heavy rainfall, prolonged calm conditions and heat waves – could still impact the dead zone’s size and duration.

The 2025 dead zone was right around average as high amounts of spring rainfall were offset by a cooler, drier and unusually breezy summer, officials said.
